claim: Over half of breast-cancer-related deaths are due to recurrence 5 or more years after initial diagnosis and treatment.
source: Over half of breast-cancer-related deaths are due to recurrence 5 or more years after initial diagnosis and treatment.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sosa et al., 2014 in the Introduction section.

claim: Her2 downregulation leads to an inflammatory program driven by TNFα/NFκB signaling.
source: Her2 downregulation leads to an inflammatory program driven by TNFα/NFκB signaling, which promotes immune cell infiltration in regressing and residual tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data showing enrichment of inflammatory and TNFα/NFκB gene signatures following Her2 downregulation, and by experimental data showing TNFα expression increases and IKK inhibition blocks chemokine induction.

claim: CCL5 is elevated following Her2 downregulation and remains high in residual tumors.
source: The cytokine CCL5 is elevated following Her2 downregulation and remains high in residual tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data, qPCR analysis, cytokine arrays, and ELISA measurements showing CCL5 upregulation after Her2 downregulation and in residual tumors.

claim: CCL5 promotes tumor recurrence by recruiting CCR5-expressing macrophages.
source: CCL5 promotes tumor recurrence by recruiting CCR5-expressing macrophages, which may contribute to collagen deposition in residual tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by orthotopic recurrence assays showing CCL5 overexpression accelerates recurrence, flow cytometry showing increased macrophage infiltration in CCL5-expressing tumors, and CCR5 expression analysis on macrophages.

claim: An E2F signature was the most highly enriched gene set in cells with Her2 signaling on.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis showed that an E2F signature was the most highly enriched gene set in cells with Her2 signaling on (+dox; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), consistent with previous literature and the observation that Her2 is required for the proliferation of these cells (Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis of RNA-seq data and is consistent with cited literature (Lee et al., 2000).

claim: The gene sets most significantly enriched in cells following Her2 downregulation were an inflammatory gene signature and a TNFα/NFκB gene signature.
source: Interestingly, the gene sets most significantly enriched in cells following Her2 downregulation (-dox) were an inflammatory gene signature and a TNFα/NFκB gene signature (Figure 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by GSEA analysis shown in Figure 1B.

claim: Genes encoding chemokines in the CCL family (CCL2, CCL5, and CCL20) and CXCL family (CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL3, CXCL5, and CXCL10) were upregulated following Her2 downregulation.
source: These gene sets comprised genes encoding chemokines in the CCL family (CCL2, CCL5, and CCL20) and CXCL family (CXCL1, CXCL2, CXCL3, CXCL5, and CXCL10), proteins that mediate cell-cell interactions (TLR2, ICAM1, and CSF1) as well as signaling components of the NFκB pathway (NFΚBIA and NFΚBIE). All these genes were upregulated following Her2 downregulation (Figure 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 1C.

claim: Treatment with conditioned media from Her2-off cells led to time-dependent upregulation of CCL5.
source: Treatment with conditioned media led to a time-dependent upregulation of the pro-inflammatory chemokine CCL5 (Figure 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR analysis shown in Figure 1D.

claim: TNFα expression is increased between 10-fold and 100-fold following Her2 downregulation.
source: One common upstream mediator of this cytokine response is tumor necrosis factor alpha (TNFα), and we found that TNFα expression is increased between 10-fold and 100-fold following Her2 downregulation (Figure 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1E.

claim: Treatment of naive cells with Her2-off conditioned media led to rapid, robust, and prolonged activation of the NFκB pathway as assessed by phosphorylation of p65.
source: Indeed, we found that treatment of naive cells with Her2-off (–dox) conditioned media led to rapid, robust, and prolonged activation of the NFκB pathway as assessed by phosphorylation of p65 (Figure 1F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot analysis shown in Figure 1F.

claim: Blocking IKK activity blunted the induction of all chemokine genes following dox withdrawal.
source: Finally, we tested whether the induction of chemokine genes following Her2 downregulation was dependent upon the NFκB pathway by treating cells with the IKK inhibitor, IKK16. We found that blocking IKK activity blunted the induction of all chemokine genes following dox withdrawal (Figure 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data with IKK16 treatment shown in Figure 1G.

claim: Neratinib treatment led to an increase in phospho-p65.
source: Neratinib treatment led to an increase in phospho-p65 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C), increased expression of TNFα (Figure 1—figure supplement 1D), and increased expression of the NFκB targets CXCL5 and CCL5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E and F).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1C.

claim: Dox treatment had no effect on the induction of NFκB target genes following TNFα treatment in NIH3T3 cells.
source: To further confirm that the low concentrations of dox used to culture primary tumor cells do not directly inhibit the NFκB pathway we treated NIH3T3 cells with TNFα in the presence or absence of 2 μg/ml dox and measured NFκB target genes. Dox treatment had no effect on the induction of NFκB target genes following TNFα treatment (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G.

claim: Leukocyte infiltration increased dramatically following Her2 downregulation as compared to primary tumors.
source: CD45 staining showed that leukocyte infiltration increased dramatically following Her2 downregulation as compared to primary tumors (Figure 2B–C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD45 immunohistochemistry shown in Figures 2B-C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Leukocytes remained high in residual tumors.
source: Surprisingly, leukocytes remained high in residual tumors (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD45 immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Masson's trichrome staining revealed prominent collagen deposition in residual tumors.
source: Masson's trichrome staining revealed prominent collagen deposition in residual tumors (Figure 2D), consistent with a desmoplastic response in residual tumors.
evidence: This claim is supported by Masson's trichrome staining shown in Figure 2D.

claim: Macrophage abundance increased dramatically during tumor regression.
source: Staining for the macrophage marker F4/80 showed a dramatic increase in macrophage abundance during tumor regression (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and macrophage levels remained elevated in residual tumors (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by F4/80 immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2C and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: Macrophage levels remained elevated in residual tumors.
source: Staining for the macrophage marker F4/80 showed a dramatic increase in macrophage abundance during tumor regression (Figure 2C, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A), and macrophage levels remained elevated in residual tumors (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by F4/80 immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A.

claim: CD3 staining showed increased T cell infiltration in regressing and residual tumors.
source: CD3 staining showed increased T cell infiltration in regressing and residual tumors (Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B).
evidence: This claim is supported by CD3 immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A,B.

claim: Eight cytokines were upregulated in residual tumors as compared to primary tumors (fold change >2, p < 0.1).
source: This analysis identified eight cytokines that were upregulated in residual tumors as compared to primary tumors (Figure 3A; fold change >2, p < 0.1, Figure 3—source data 1), including CCL5, osteoprotegerin (OPG), and Vascular cell adhesion protein 1 (VCAM-1) (Figure 3B).
evidence: This claim is supported by cytokine array data shown in Figure 3A and 3B.

claim: VCAM-1 has been shown to regulate breast cancer dormancy.
source: Interestingly, VCAM-1 has been shown to regulate breast cancer dormancy (Lu et al., 2011), while OPG can regulate the survival of breast cancer cells (Neville-Webbe et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2011.

claim: OPG can regulate the survival of breast cancer cells.
source: Interestingly, VCAM-1 has been shown to regulate breast cancer dormancy (Lu et al., 2011), while OPG can regulate the survival of breast cancer cells (Neville-Webbe et al., 2004).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Neville-Webbe et al., 2004.

claim: CCL5 was one of the most significantly upregulated cytokines in human residual breast tumors following neoadjuvant targeted therapy.
source: We analyzed a gene expression dataset of residual breast tumors that remain following neoadjuvant targeted therapy. A number of secreted factors were upregulated in residual tumors as compared to primary tumors, and CCL5 was one of the most significantly upregulated cytokines in this group (Figure 3C–D and Figure 3—figure supplement 1A–M).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of gene expression dataset GSE10281 shown in Figures 3C-D.

claim: CCL5 expression was increased in residual tumors in an independent dataset from breast cancer patients treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
source: To confirm these results, we examined an independent gene expression data set from breast cancer patients treated with neoadjuvant chemotherapy. We found that CCL5 expression was also increased in residual tumors in this dataset (Figure 3—figure supplement 1N).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of gene expression dataset GSE21974 shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1N.

claim: CCL5 expression was elevated in residual tumors as measured by ELISA.
source: We first used an ELISA to measure CCL5 levels in orthotopic primary tumors, residual tumors, and recurrent tumors. CCL5 expression was elevated in residual tumors, confirming results from the cytokine array, and increased further in recurrent tumors (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: Tumors expressing CCL5 recurred significantly earlier than control tumors.
source: Tumors expressing CCL5 recurred significantly earlier than control tumors, indicating that CCL5 expression is sufficient to accelerate tumor recurrence (Figure 4C; p = 0.023; HR = 2.14).
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4C.

claim: CCL5 knockout had no effect on the latency of recurrence.
source: Mice were removed from dox, and the latency of recurrence between control and CCL5 knockout tumors was compared. We found that CCL5 knockout had no effect on the latency of recurrence (Figure 4E).
evidence: This claim is supported by Kaplan-Meier survival analysis shown in Figure 4E.

claim: The level of CCR5 expressed on macrophages increased in residual tumors.
source: Interestingly, the level of CCR5 expressed on macrophages increased in residual tumors (Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5A and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: CCR5 expression on CD4+ T cells and CD8+ T cells increased in regressing tumors, but returned to baseline in residual tumors.
source: In contrast, CCR5 expression on CD4+ T cells CD8+ T cells increased in regressing tumors, but returned to baseline in residual tumors (Figure 5B and C, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figures 5B and C, and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: The expression of CCR5 on fibroblasts was elevated in residual tumors.
source: Similar to macrophages, the expression of CCR5 on fibroblasts was elevated in residual tumors (Figure 5D, Figure 5—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5D and Figure 5—figure supplement 2.

claim: CCR5 was expressed at higher levels on macrophages than tumor cells at each stage.
source: To directly compare the expression of CCR5 in macrophages and tumor cells, we sorted these two populations from primary, regressing, residual, and recurrent tumors from MTB;TAN mice and performed qPCR analysis. CCR5 was expressed at higher levels on macrophages than tumor cells at each stage, and its expression was especially high on residual tumor macrophages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR analysis of sorted cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Fibroblast levels were not significantly different between control and CCL5-expressing tumors.
source: To determine whether these cell types are recruited by CCL5 in residual tumors, we generated primary and residual tumors overexpressing CCL5 and analyzed the abundance of macrophages and fibroblasts by flow cytometry. Fibroblast levels were not significantly different between control and CCL5-expressing tumors (Figure 5F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1C).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5F and Figure 5—figure supplement 1C.

claim: CCL5-expressing tumors exhibited a modest but consistent increase in macrophage infiltration.
source: In contrast, CCL5-expressing tumors exhibited a modest but consistent increase in macrophage infiltration (Figure 5G, Figure 5—figure supplement 1D).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5G and Figure 5—figure supplement 1D.

claim: Genes encoding fibrillar collagen and collagen deposition proteins were more highly expressed in recurrent TAMs than primary TAMs or regressing tumor TAMs.
source: Interestingly, genes encoding fibrillar collagen and collagen deposition proteins were more highly expressed in the recurrent TAMs than the primary TAMs or regressing tumor TAMs (Figure 6B).
evidence: This claim is supported by RNA-seq data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The expression of collagen genes (COL5A1, COL24A1, ASPN, PCOLCE) progressively increased during tumor regression, residual disease, and recurrence in TAMs.
source: We next sought to validate these findings by performing qPCR analysis on primary, regressing, residual, and recurrent TAMs. This analysis showed that the expression of these genes progressively increased during tumor regression, residual disease, and recurrence (Figure 6C).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Masson's trichrome staining showed increased collagen deposition in residual and recurrent tumors.
source: Consistent with this, Masson's trichrome staining showed increased collagen deposition in residual and recurrent tumors (Figure 6E, middle and bottom).
evidence: This claim is supported by Masson's trichrome staining shown in Figure 6E.

claim: Expression of collagen genes (ASPN, COL5A1, COL24A1, PCOLCE) increased in human residual tumors following neoadjuvant targeted therapy.
source: In order to see if similar gene expression patterns are observed in residual disease in breast cancer patients, we examined gene expression data from residual tumors after neoadjuvant targeted therapy. Indeed, expression of these four collagen genes increased in residual tumors following therapy (Figure 6—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by analysis of gene expression dataset GSE10281 shown in Figure 6—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A subset of CCL5-expressing tumors had very high levels of collagen deposition.
source: Finally, we asked whether CCL5 regulates collagen deposition by comparing collagen levels in control and CCL5-expressing recurrent tumors. While control recurrent tumors had uniform levels of collagen deposition (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C), a subset of CCL5-expressing tumors had very high levels of collagen deposition (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Masson's trichrome staining shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: Her2 downregulation in Her2-driven tumors in vivo induces apoptosis and growth arrest, ultimately leading to tumor regression.
source: Her2 downregulation in Her2-driven tumors in vivo induces apoptosis and growth arrest, ultimately leading to tumor regression (Moody et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Moody et al., 2002.

claim: A small population of tumor cells can survive Her2 downregulation and persist for up to 6 months before resuming growth to form recurrent tumors.
source: However, a small population of tumor cells can survive Her2 downregulation and persist for up to 6 months before resuming growth to form recurrent tumors.
evidence: This claim is based on observations from the MTB;TAN mouse model described in the manuscript.

claim: Residual tumors contain high numbers of macrophages and abundant collagen deposition, consistent with a desmoplastic response.
source: Taken together, these results indicate that Her2 downregulation leads to the infiltration of CD45+ leukocytes, and specifically F4/80+ macrophages. Residual tumors contain high numbers of macrophages and abundant collagen deposition, consistent with a desmoplastic response.
evidence: This claim is supported by immunohistochemistry and Masson's trichrome staining data shown in Figure 2.

claim: CCL5 expression is sufficient to accelerate tumor recurrence.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that CCL5 expression is sufficient to accelerate recurrence, but tumor-derived CCL5 is not necessary for recurrence following Her2 downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by orthotopic recurrence assays showing CCL5 overexpression accelerates recurrence (Figure 4C).

claim: Tumor-derived CCL5 is not necessary for recurrence following Her2 downregulation.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that CCL5 expression is sufficient to accelerate recurrence, but tumor-derived CCL5 is not necessary for recurrence following Her2 downregulation.
evidence: This claim is supported by orthotopic recurrence assays showing CCL5 knockout had no effect on recurrence latency (Figure 4E).

claim: CCL5 is a chemoattractant for various cell types, including T cells, B cells, eosinophils, basophils, neutrophils, macrophages, and fibroblasts.
source: CCL5 is a chemoattractant for various cell types, including T cells, B cells, eosinophils, basophils, neutrophils, macrophages, and fibroblasts (Dembic, 2015; Lacy, 2017; Lee et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Dembic, 2015; Lacy, 2017; Lee et al., 2017.

claim: CCL5 predominately acts through CCR5.
source: CCL5 can signal through multiple receptors, including CCR1, CCR3, and CCR5, but it predominately acts through CCR5 (Soria and Ben-Baruch, 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Soria and Ben-Baruch, 2008.

claim: CCL5 expression in residual tumors can recruit CCR5-positive macrophages.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that CCL5 expression in residual tumors can recruit CCR5-positive macrophages, and suggest that CCL5 may subsequently signal through CCR5 on these cells to modulate macrophage function.
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data showing increased macrophage infiltration in CCL5-expressing tumors (Figure 5G) and CCR5 expression on macrophages (Figure 5A).

claim: CCL5 may signal through CCR5 on macrophages to modulate macrophage function.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that CCL5 expression in residual tumors can recruit CCR5-positive macrophages, and suggest that CCL5 may subsequently signal through CCR5 on these cells to modulate macrophage function.
evidence: This is a speculative claim based on the observation that CCL5 recruits CCR5+ macrophages.

claim: Collagen deposition can be mediated in part through CCR2+ macrophages in colorectal cancer.
source: This is reminiscent of findings in colorectal cancer, where collagen deposition can be mediated in part through CCR2+ macrophages, and depletion of these macrophages inhibits tumor growth (Afik et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Afik et al., 2016.

claim: Depletion of CCR2+ macrophages inhibits tumor growth in colorectal cancer.
source: This is reminiscent of findings in colorectal cancer, where collagen deposition can be mediated in part through CCR2+ macrophages, and depletion of these macrophages inhibits tumor growth (Afik et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Afik et al., 2016.

claim: Her2 signaling directly activates the NFκB pathway.
source: A number of studies have found that Her2 signaling directly activates the NFκB pathway, and that this is functionally important for tumor growth (Liu et al., 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2009.

claim: The NFκB pathway is required for macrophage recruitment in a Her2-driven mouse model.
source: These findings are consistent with prior work showing that the NFκB pathway is required for macrophage recruitment in a similar Her2-driven mouse model (Liu et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Liu et al., 2010.

claim: CCL5 has been shown to play an important role in invasion, metastasis, neoangiogenesis, and immune cell infiltration.
source: CCL5 has been shown to play an important role in many facets of tumor progression, such as invasion, metastasis, neoangiogenesis, and immune cell infiltration (Aldinucci and Colombatti, 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Aldinucci and Colombatti, 2014.

claim: In glioblastoma, CCL5 upregulation has been correlated with recurrence in post-treatment tumors.
source: In glioblastoma, CCL5 upregulation has been correlated with recurrence in post-treatment tumors (Hudson et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Hudson et al., 2018.

claim: In triple-negative breast cancer, CCL5 expression has been correlated with residual tumor size and tumor infiltrating lymphocytes after neoadjuvant chemotherapy.
source: In triple-negative breast cancer, CCL5 expression has also been correlated with residual tumor size and tumor infiltrating lymphocytes after neoadjuvant chemotherapy (Araujo et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Araujo et al., 2018.

claim: CCL5 may be at least partially redundant with other chemokines in recruiting macrophages to promote recurrence.
source: A notable observation in our study is that while CCL5 expression promoted recurrence (Figure 4C), knockout of CCL5 in tumor cells did not delay recurrence (Figure 4E). This suggests that CCL5 may be at least partially redundant with other chemokines, such as CCL2 and CXCL1 and 2, in recruiting macrophages to promote recurrence.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that CCL5 overexpression promotes recurrence but knockout does not delay it.

claim: Collagen deposition is traditionally thought to be driven by fibroblasts in the microenvironment.
source: Collagen deposition is traditionally thought to be driven by fibroblasts in the microenvironment (Thannickal, 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Thannickal, 2012.

claim: Macrophages are responsible for collagen deposition in a mouse model of colorectal cancer.
source: However, a recent report showed that macrophages are responsible for collagen deposition in a mouse model of colorectal cancer (Afik et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Afik et al., 2016.

claim: Collagen deposition is important for tumor progression and invasiveness.
source: Collagen deposition is important for tumor progression and invasiveness (Provenzano et al., 2008).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Provenzano et al., 2008.

claim: Enzymes which crosslink collagens are often upregulated in breast cancer and are correlated with a poor prognosis.
source: Collagen bundles can potentiate cell migration and increase tissue stiffness, and enzymes which crosslink collagens are often upregulated in breast cancer and are correlated with a poor prognosis (Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lu et al., 2012.

claim: Collagen deposition may promote the survival or proliferation of residual tumor cells.
source: It is possible that collagen deposition may promote the survival or proliferation of residual tumor cells, and that this mediates the effect of CCL5 on tumor recurrence.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about the mechanism by which CCL5 promotes recurrence.

claim: Breast cancer cells can express CCR5.
source: It is important to note that while our studies focus on the function of CCL5 in recruiting CCR5+ macrophages, breast cancer cells themselves can also express CCR5.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the Discussion.

claim: CCR5 acts in tumor cells to promote stem cell expansion and metastasis in breast cancer.
source: Indeed, previous studies have found that CCR5 acts in tumor cells to promote stem cell expansion and metastasis in breast cancer (Jiao et al., 2018; Velasco-Velázquez et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Jiao et al., 2018 and Velasco-Velázquez et al., 2012.

claim: In residual tumors CCR5 is expressed at higher levels in macrophages than on tumor cells.
source: Although in the current study we find that in residual tumors CCR5 is expressed at higher levels in macrophages than on tumor cells, it is possible that tumor cell-expressed CCR5 may mediate at least some of the effects of CCL5 on tumor recurrence.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Tumor cell-expressed CCR5 may mediate at least some of the effects of CCL5 on tumor recurrence.
source: Although in the current study we find that in residual tumors CCR5 is expressed at higher levels in macrophages than on tumor cells, it is possible that tumor cell-expressed CCR5 may mediate at least some of the effects of CCL5 on tumor recurrence.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential mechanisms.

claim: Interactions between residual tumor cells and their microenvironment are critical for recurrent tumor formation.
source: The results identified here show that interactions between residual tumor cells and their microenvironment are critical for recurrent tumor formation.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on the overall findings of the study.

claim: Targeting tumor cell-microenvironment interactions may hold promise for preventing recurrent breast cancer.
source: Targeting tumor cell-microenvironment interactions may hold promise for preventing recurrent breast cancer.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential therapeutic applications.

claim: Approximately 270,000 women will be diagnosed with breast cancer in 2018.
source: In 2018, it is estimated that approximately 270,000 women will be diagnosed with breast cancer, and 41,000 women will succumb to the disease (Siegel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2018.

claim: Approximately 41,000 women will succumb to breast cancer in 2018.
source: In 2018, it is estimated that approximately 270,000 women will be diagnosed with breast cancer, and 41,000 women will succumb to the disease (Siegel et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Siegel et al., 2018.

claim: The long latency of recurrence has led to speculation that residual tumor cells are slowly growing or even dormant.
source: The long latency of recurrence has led to speculation that residual tumor cells are slowly growing or even dormant (Hölzel et al., 2010; Klein, 2009).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Hölzel et al., 2010 and Klein, 2009.

claim: Genetic mutations that render cells resistant to therapy represent an important mechanism of survival.
source: Genetic mutations that render cells resistant to therapy represent an important mechanism of survival (Holohan et al., 2013), but there is emerging evidence that non-genetic pathways can also promote survival in response to therapy.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Holohan et al., 2013.

claim: A population of cells called drug-tolerant persisters has been shown to survive therapy through epigenetic adaptations.
source: For instance, a population of cells called drug-tolerant persisters has been shown to survive therapy through epigenetic adaptations (Sharma et al., 2010).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sharma et al., 2010.

claim: Epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition has been shown to promote cell survival in response to EGFR inhibitors.
source: Additionally, epithelial-to-mesenchymal transition has been shown to promote cell survival in response to EGFR inhibitors (Sequist et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Sequist et al., 2011.

claim: Alterations in apoptotic pathways within tumor cells can promote cell survival in response to both chemotherapy and targeted therapy.
source: Finally, alterations in apoptotic pathways within tumor cells can promote cell survival in response to both chemotherapy and targeted therapy (Alvarez et al., 2013; Damrauer et al., 2018; Hata et al., 2016; Holohan et al., 2013; Mabe et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alvarez et al., 2013; Damrauer et al., 2018; Hata et al., 2016; Holohan et al., 2013; Mabe et al., 2018.

claim: Administration of doxycycline to bitransgenic MMTV-rtTA;TetO-Her2/neu (MTB;TAN) mice leads to mammary gland-specific expression of Her2 and the development of Her2-driven tumors.
source: In this model, administration of doxycycline (dox) to bitransgenic MMTV-rtTA;TetO-Her2/neu (MTB;TAN) mice leads to mammary gland-specific expression of epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (Her2) and the development of Her2-driven tumors.
evidence: This describes the experimental model used in the study.

claim: Removal of dox induces Her2 downregulation and tumor regression in the MTB;TAN model.
source: Removal of dox induces Her2 downregulation and tumor regression.
evidence: This describes the experimental model used in the study.

claim: A small population of residual tumor cells can survive and persist in a non-proliferative state in the MTB;TAN model.
source: However, a small population of residual tumor cells can survive and persist in a non-proliferative state (Alvarez et al., 2013; Moody et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alvarez et al., 2013 and Moody et al., 2002.

claim: Residual cells eventually re-initiate proliferation to form recurrent tumors that are independent of Her2.
source: These cells eventually re-initiate proliferation to form recurrent tumors that are independent of Her2.
evidence: This describes the behavior of residual cells in the MTB;TAN model.

claim: A recent study identified a similar gene expression program in EGFR-mutant lung cancer following treatment with EGFR inhibitors.
source: Notably, a recent study identified a similar gene expression program in EGFR-mutant lung cancer following treatment with EGFR inhibitors (Gong et al., 2018).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Gong et al., 2018.

claim: At high concentrations (>40 μg/ml) doxycycline can inhibit the NFκB pathway.
source: At high concentrations (>40 μg/ml) doxycycline itself can inhibit the NFκB pathway (Alexander-Savino et al., 2016; Santa-Cecília et al., 2016).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Alexander-Savino et al., 2016 and Santa-Cecília et al., 2016.

claim: The concentrations of dox (2 μg/ml) used to culture primary tumor cells are well below levels that inhibit NFκB.
source: Although the concentrations of dox (2 μg/ml) we use to culture primary tumor cells are well below these levels, we wanted to confirmed that the NFκB pathway activation observed following dox withdrawal was due to loss of Her2 signaling.
evidence: This is a statement about the experimental conditions used in the study.

claim: Her2 is required for the proliferation of Her2-driven tumor cells.
source: Gene set enrichment analysis showed that an E2F signature was the most highly enriched gene set in cells with Her2 signaling on (+dox; Figure 1—figure supplement 1B), consistent with previous literature and the observation that Her2 is required for the proliferation of these cells (Lee et al., 2000).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Lee et al., 2000 and is consistent with the E2F signature enrichment.

claim: Her2 levels remained high in cells treated with Her2-off conditioned media supplemented with dox.
source: Importantly, Her2 levels remained high in these target cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), indicating that Her2-off (–dox) conditioned media can activate the NFκB pathway even in the presence of Her2 signaling.
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1H.

claim: Her2-off conditioned media can activate the NFκB pathway even in the presence of Her2 signaling.
source: Importantly, Her2 levels remained high in these target cells (Figure 1—figure supplement 1H), indicating that Her2-off (–dox) conditioned media can activate the NFκB pathway even in the presence of Her2 signaling.
evidence: This is an inference based on the observation that conditioned media activates NFκB in cells with high Her2 expression.

claim: Conditioned media from Her2-on cells had no effect on p65 phosphorylation.
source: In contrast, conditioned media from Her2-on (+dox) cells had no effect on p65 phosphorylation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1I).
evidence: This claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1I.

claim: Her2 downregulation leads to the induction of a pro-inflammatory gene expression program, likely driven by autocrine-acting TNFα and mediated through the IKK-NFκB pathway.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that Her2 downregulation leads to the induction of a pro-inflammatory gene expression program, likely driven by autocrine-acting TNFα and mediated through the IKK-NFκB pathway.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on multiple experimental results including RNA-seq, qPCR, Western blots, and IKK inhibition experiments.

claim: Many of the cytokines and chemokines induced shortly after Her2 downregulation function as chemoattractants for various immune cells.
source: Many of the cytokines and chemokines induced shortly after Her2 downregulation function as chemoattractants for various immune cells (Binnewies et al., 2018; López et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Binnewies et al., 2018 and López et al., 2017.

claim: Only two cytokines, CCL5 and OPG, were both induced acutely following Her2 downregulation and remained elevated in residual tumors.
source: We next asked whether any cytokines were both induced acutely following Her2 downregulation and remained elevated in residual tumors. We found that only two cytokines, CCL5 and OPG, fulfilled these criteria.
evidence: This claim is based on comparison of RNA-seq data from cells and cytokine array data from tumors.

claim: CCL5 upregulation is a common feature of residual tumor cells that survive both conventional and targeted therapy in mice and humans.
source: These results suggest that CCL5 upregulation is a common feature of residual tumors cells that survive both conventional and targeted therapy in mice and humans, suggesting it may be functionally important in mediating the survival of these cells.
evidence: This claim is based on analysis of multiple datasets including mouse orthotopic tumors and human gene expression datasets GSE10281 and GSE21974.

claim: CCL5 expression increased further in recurrent tumors compared to residual tumors.
source: We first used an ELISA to measure CCL5 levels in orthotopic primary tumors, residual tumors, and recurrent tumors. CCL5 expression was elevated in residual tumors, confirming results from the cytokine array, and increased further in recurrent tumors (Figure 4A).
evidence: This claim is supported by ELISA data shown in Figure 4A.

claim: CCL5 expression had no effect on the growth of primary tumors.
source: Primary tumors formed with similar kinetics following injection of control and CCL5-expressing cells, indicating that CCL5 expression had no effect on the growth of primary tumors (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of tumor growth kinetics, though the data is not shown.

claim: The growth of CCL5 knockout tumors was not different from control tumors.
source: The growth of CCL5 knockout tumors was not different from control tumors expressing a non-targeting sgRNA (data not shown).
evidence: This claim is based on observation of tumor growth, though the data is not shown.

claim: Her2 was downregulated following dox withdrawal in all tumors analyzed by flow cytometry.
source: As expected, Her2 was downregulated following dox withdrawal in all tumors (Figure 5—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by qRT-PCR data shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1A.

claim: A slight increase in CCR5 expression was observed in residual tumor cells.
source: We were also interested in examining CCR5 expression on CD45– tumor cells. We observed a slight increase in CCR5 expression in residual tumor cells, but otherwise there was no change in CCR5 expression on these cells (Figure 5E).
evidence: This claim is supported by flow cytometry data shown in Figure 5E.

claim: CCR5 expression was especially high on residual tumor macrophages.
source: To directly compare the expression of CCR5 in macrophages and tumor cells, we sorted these two populations from primary, regressing, residual, and recurrent tumors from MTB;TAN mice and performed qPCR analysis. CCR5 was expressed at higher levels on macrophages than tumor cells at each stage, and its expression was especially high on residual tumor macrophages (Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data on sorted cells shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: Residual tumor-associated macrophages did not yield sufficient RNA for RNAseq.
source: Residual tumor-associated macrophages did not yield sufficient RNA for RNAseq, but we were able to sequence RNA from primary, regressing, and recurrent tumor-associated macrophages (TAMs).
evidence: This is a statement about technical limitations of the study.

claim: FACS-sorted TAMs may have been partially contaminated with tumor cells.
source: Examination of differentially expressed genes between primary and recurrent TAMs suggested that FACS-sorted TAMs may have been partially contaminated with tumor cells. For instance, we detected Her2 expression at high levels in primary TAMs and low levels in recurrent TAMs.
evidence: This is an inference based on detection of Her2 expression in sorted macrophages.

claim: Approximately 200 genes were differentially expressed between primary and recurrent tumor macrophages after filtering.
source: Therefore, we used a gene expression dataset of primary and recurrent tumor cells cultured in vitro to filter the TAM expression list (Figure 6—source data 1). After filtering, we were left with approximately 200 genes that were differentially expressed between primary and recurrent tumor macrophages (Figure 6A, Figure 6—source data 2).
evidence: This claim is based on RNA-seq analysis shown in Figure 6A.

claim: COL5A1 and COL24A1 encode fibrillar collagens.
source: These genes include Collagen alpha-1(V) chain (COL5A1), Collagen type XXIV alpha 1 (COL24A1), Procollagen C-endopeptidase enhancer 1 (PCOLCE), and Asporin (ASPN). COL5A1 and COL24A1 encode fibrillar collagens, PCOLCE encodes a glycoprotein that binds and drives the cleavage of type one fibrillar procollagen, and ASPN encodes a protein that binds to fibrillar collagens to regulate mineralization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of these genes.

claim: PCOLCE encodes a glycoprotein that binds and drives the cleavage of type one fibrillar procollagen.
source: These genes include Collagen alpha-1(V) chain (COL5A1), Collagen type XXIV alpha 1 (COL24A1), Procollagen C-endopeptidase enhancer 1 (PCOLCE), and Asporin (ASPN). COL5A1 and COL24A1 encode fibrillar collagens, PCOLCE encodes a glycoprotein that binds and drives the cleavage of type one fibrillar procollagen, and ASPN encodes a protein that binds to fibrillar collagens to regulate mineralization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of PCOLCE.

claim: ASPN encodes a protein that binds to fibrillar collagens to regulate mineralization.
source: These genes include Collagen alpha-1(V) chain (COL5A1), Collagen type XXIV alpha 1 (COL24A1), Procollagen C-endopeptidase enhancer 1 (PCOLCE), and Asporin (ASPN). COL5A1 and COL24A1 encode fibrillar collagens, PCOLCE encodes a glycoprotein that binds and drives the cleavage of type one fibrillar procollagen, and ASPN encodes a protein that binds to fibrillar collagens to regulate mineralization.
evidence: This is established knowledge about the function of ASPN.

claim: qPCR on RNA isolated from bulk tumors showed higher expression of COL5A1 and COL24A1 in recurrent tumors.
source: Additionally, qPCR on RNA isolated from bulk tumors showed higher expression of COL5A1 and COL24A1 in recurrent tumors, while a subset of recurrent tumors had high expression of ASPN and PCOLCE (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: A subset of recurrent tumors had high expression of ASPN and PCOLCE.
source: Additionally, qPCR on RNA isolated from bulk tumors showed higher expression of COL5A1 and COL24A1 in recurrent tumors, while a subset of recurrent tumors had high expression of ASPN and PCOLCE (Figure 6D).
evidence: This claim is supported by qPCR data shown in Figure 6D.

claim: Control recurrent tumors had uniform levels of collagen deposition.
source: Finally, we asked whether CCL5 regulates collagen deposition by comparing collagen levels in control and CCL5-expressing recurrent tumors. While control recurrent tumors had uniform levels of collagen deposition (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C), a subset of CCL5-expressing tumors had very high levels of collagen deposition (Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by Masson's trichrome staining shown in Figure 6F and Figure 6—figure supplement 1B-C.

claim: CCL5 promotes macrophage infiltration and collagen deposition.
source: Taken together, these results suggest that CCL5 promotes macrophage infiltration and collagen deposition. Given the importance of collagen for regulating tumor cell function, this may be one mechanism by which CCL5 expression accelerates recurrence.
evidence: This is a summary claim based on flow cytometry and Masson's trichrome staining data.

claim: Collagen bundles can potentiate cell migration and increase tissue stiffness.
source: Collagen bundles can potentiate cell migration and increase tissue stiffness, and enzymes which crosslink collagens are often upregulated in breast cancer and are correlated with a poor prognosis (Lu et al., 2012).
evidence: This is established knowledge about collagen function, supported by citation to Lu et al., 2012.

claim: Blocking the TNFα-CCL5-macrophage axis may be efficacious in preventing breast cancer recurrence.
source: Blocking this TNFα-CCL5-macrophage axis may be efficacious in preventing breast cancer recurrence.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential therapeutic applications based on the study findings.

claim: Maraviroc is a CCR5 antagonist.
source: Possible therapies include the use of Maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist (Velasco-Velázquez et al., 2012), and agents that block macrophage infiltration or function, such as the CSF-1R inhibitor PLX3397 (DeNardo et al., 2011; Strachan et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Velasco-Velázquez et al., 2012.

claim: PLX3397 is a CSF-1R inhibitor that blocks macrophage infiltration or function.
source: Possible therapies include the use of Maraviroc, a CCR5 antagonist (Velasco-Velázquez et al., 2012), and agents that block macrophage infiltration or function, such as the CSF-1R inhibitor PLX3397 (DeNardo et al., 2011; Strachan et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2014).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to DeNardo et al., 2011; Strachan et al., 2013; Zhu et al., 2014.

claim: It may be preferable to block the induction of the pro-inflammatory program using agents targeting TNFα or the NFκB pathway.
source: It is also possible that, because CCL5 is sufficient but not necessary for tumor recurrence, it would be preferable to block the induction of the pro-inflammatory program that is induced following Her2 downregulation using agents targeting TNFα or the NFκB pathway.
evidence: This is a speculative claim about potential therapeutic strategies.
